html:
Between 1609 and 1621 the Dutch East India Company conquered the Banda Islands in eastern Indonesia, killing, enslaving or driving out most of their people. The goal was a monopoly on nutmeg and mace, which then grew only on these small islands.

The Bandanese were traders who sold to all comers, including the English, and resisted Dutch demands to sell only to them. Talks broke down in 1609 when Bandanese elders killed a Dutch admiral and his men. In 1621 governor general Jan Pieterszoon Coen invaded with a large force including Japanese mercenaries. Village leaders were executed, and the population, perhaps 15,000 before, fell to about a thousand. Many died of hunger or fled to other islands.

The company then divided the land into plantations run by Dutch planters and worked by enslaved people; see Slave trade in Dutch Asia. The English held on to tiny Run island until the Treaty of Breda of 1667, when it was left to the Dutch while England kept New Amsterdam, later New York.
